---
title: "Probability Distributions"
---

This appendix is a reference catalogue of the probability distributions used in the book. For each
family we record the support, the probability mass or density function, the mean, the variance, and the
moment generating function where it exists. The discrete families (Bernoulli, binomial, Poisson
binomial, Poisson) and the normal, multivariate normal, and standard normal are defined and their
moments derived in @sec-distributions and @sec-mvn of Chapter 4; this appendix collects those results
and adds the further families (exponential, gamma, beta, Weibull, Dirichlet) that appear later as
survival baselines in Chapters 25 and 26 and as conjugate priors in Chapter 8. Nothing here is proved
that is not proved in the chapters or that does not follow by a one-line calculation; the value of the
appendix is a single place to look up a defining formula. For the symbols used throughout, see
[Notation](/notation.qmd).

## How to read this appendix {#sec-dist-howto}

The fastest way to use this catalogue is to first name the **modeling role** you are in, then look up
the family. Every distribution in the book plays one of six roles:

1. an **outcome likelihood**, the model for the observed data on one arm of a trial (a binomial for
   responders, a Poisson for event counts, a normal for a continuous endpoint);
2. a **prior**, the distribution placed on an unknown parameter before seeing data (a beta on a
   response probability, a gamma on a rate, a normal on a treatment effect);
3. a **covariate model**, the distribution of baseline patient characteristics (a multivariate normal
   for correlated covariates);
4. a **discrete aggregation device**, used to turn individual-level risks into an aggregate event count
   (the Poisson binomial and its Poisson approximation in Part V);
5. a **survival baseline**, the model for a time-to-event outcome (exponential, Weibull); or
6. a **numerical integration device**, used to average an individual likelihood over a covariate
   distribution (the standard normal and the Gaussian copula in the ML-NMR integration of Chapter 22).

@tbl-dist-roles maps each family to the clinical object it typically models and to the chapters that use
it. A reader browsing this appendix should start there, identify the role, and then read only the
relevant catalogue entry.

| Distribution | Typical health-data object | Role in this book | Where it appears |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bernoulli, binomial | responders out of randomized patients (binary endpoint) | outcome likelihood | Ch. 4, 7, 13; Part V |
| Poisson | event counts, or events per person-time | outcome likelihood | Ch. 7; count aggregation @sec-poisson-aggregate |
| Poisson binomial | aggregate event count from patients with unequal risks | discrete aggregation device | @sec-pobin (Ch. 21) |
| Multinomial | counts across more than two response categories | outcome likelihood | Ch. 8 conjugacy |
| Normal | a continuous endpoint; an estimated log-effect; a prior | likelihood, approximate likelihood, prior | Ch. 4, 6, 8, 13 |
| Multivariate normal | correlated baseline covariates; random effects; copula scores | covariate model, random-effects prior, integration device | Ch. 4, 8; @sec-qmc-gaussian (Ch. 22) |
| Beta | a single response probability | prior on a probability | Ch. 8 |
| Dirichlet | a vector of category probabilities summing to one | prior on a probability vector | Ch. 8; this appendix |
| Gamma | a positive rate, or a precision | prior on a rate or precision; survival baseline | Ch. 8; Ch. 25, 26 |
| Exponential | time to event with constant hazard | survival baseline | Ch. 25, 26 |
| Weibull | time to event with a rising or falling hazard | survival baseline | @sec-genlik-survival (Ch. 25), 26 |
| Standard normal $\Phi,\phi$ | probit link; normal scores for QMC integration | link function, integration device | Ch. 7; @sec-qmc-pit, @sec-qmc-gaussian (Ch. 22) |

: Distribution-to-role map. Read this first: name the role (likelihood, prior, covariate model,
aggregation device, survival baseline, integration device), then read the matching catalogue entry.
{#tbl-dist-roles}

## Conventions {#sec-dist-conventions}

Three plain-language reminders precede the formulas, because the tables below mix objects of different
kinds. The **support** of a distribution is the set of values the random variable can actually take,
that is, the values where the mass or density is positive; everything outside the support has
probability zero (for a binomial the support is $\{0,1,\dots,n\}$, for a Weibull survival time it is
$(0,\infty)$). A **mass function** $P(X=k)$ gives a genuine probability at each point of a discrete
support and never exceeds $1$. A **density** $f(x)$ does not: it is a rate of probability per unit
length, and an actual probability is recovered only by integrating $f$ over an interval, so a density
can exceed $1$ (a tightly concentrated normal has a peak above $1$) even though no probability ever
does. This is why a density value is not itself a probability.

The **moment generating function** (MGF) of a random vector $X$ is
$M_X(\mathbf{t})=\mathbb{E}[e^{\mathbf{t}^{\top}X}]$, written $M_X(t)=\mathbb{E}[e^{tX}]$ in the scalar
case (@def-mgf). We say the MGF *exists* when it is finite for all $\mathbf{t}$ in an open neighborhood
of the origin; in that case it determines all moments by differentiation at the origin
(@thm-mgf-moments) and determines the law uniquely (@thm-mgf-uniqueness). Intuitively the MGF is a
bookkeeping device: because $\frac{d}{dt}e^{tX}=X e^{tX}$, each derivative evaluated at $t=0$ pulls down
one extra factor of $X$, so $M_X^{(r)}(0)=\mathbb{E}[X^{r}]$ and the entire sequence of moments is
stored in one function. That is the only reason the MGF earns a column in the tables below: given the
MGF, the mean and variance are two derivatives away. For some families with a finite MGF the function
has no elementary closed form; for the beta and Weibull families this is noted in the catalogue, and for
the Dirichlet the joint MGF on the ambient space is degenerate.

*(Advanced; skip on a first pass.)* "Degenerate on the ambient space" means the following. When the
support lies in a hyperplane, as it does for the Dirichlet whose components satisfy $\sum_k x_k=1$, one
coordinate is fixed by the others, namely $x_K=1-\sum_{k<K}x_k$. The joint MGF on $\mathbb{R}^{K}$ is
then really a function of only $K-1$ free arguments and cannot characterize the law in the usual
full-rank way, so we describe such a family by its moments instead of by an MGF. This is why the
Dirichlet row lists moments rather than an MGF.

Two special functions recur. The **gamma function** is
$$
\Gamma(s)=\int_0^{\infty} u^{s-1}e^{-u}\,du,\qquad s>0,
$$ {#eq-dist-gamma-function}
which satisfies $\Gamma(s+1)=s\,\Gamma(s)$ and $\Gamma(n)=(n-1)!$ for positive integers $n$; it is the
continuous interpolation of the factorial and appears in the normalizing constants of the gamma, beta,
Weibull, and Dirichlet densities. The **beta function** is
$$
B(a,b)=\int_0^1 u^{a-1}(1-u)^{b-1}\,du=\frac{\Gamma(a)\,\Gamma(b)}{\Gamma(a+b)},\qquad a,b>0,
$$ {#eq-dist-beta-function}
and its multivariate form, used by the Dirichlet density, is
$B(\boldsymbol{\alpha})=\prod_{k=1}^K\Gamma(\alpha_k)\big/\Gamma\!\big(\sum_{k=1}^K\alpha_k\big)$; the
scalar $B(a,b)$ is the $K=2$ case of the vector $B(\boldsymbol{\alpha})$, so the two share a symbol on
purpose. The numerical evaluation of these functions, together with the error function below, is treated
in [Appendix D](/appendices/D-special-functions.qmd).

We fix two parametrization conventions that are sources of confusion across the literature. The gamma
and exponential families are parametrized by a **rate**, so that
$\mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha,\beta)$ has shape $\alpha$, rate $\beta$, and mean $\alpha/\beta$; this matches
the convention of @prp-conjugate-gamma-poisson in Chapter 8. The Weibull family is parametrized by a
shape and a **scale**, related to the proportional-hazards parametrization of Chapter 25 as recorded
below. A rate has units of events per unit of the variable, so a larger rate means shorter times; a
scale has the units of the variable itself, so a larger scale means longer times. Because closely
related survival families are written with a rate, a scale, or a hazard depending on the chapter,
@tbl-dist-param gathers the three side by side.

| Family | Parameters (this book) | Symbols | Mean in terms of them |
|---|---|---|---|
| Exponential | rate | $\lambda$ | $1/\lambda$ |
| Gamma | shape, rate | $\alpha,\ \beta$ | $\alpha/\beta$ |
| Weibull (this appendix) | shape, scale | $k,\ \lambda$ | $\lambda\,\Gamma(1+1/k)$ |
| Weibull (Chapter 25 hazard form) | shape, rate-type coefficient | $\nu,\ \lambda(\mathbf{x})$ | via $S(t)=\exp(-\lambda(\mathbf{x})\,t^{\nu})$ |
| Normal | mean, variance | $\mu,\ \sigma^{2}$ | $\mu$ |

: Parametrization cheat sheet. The gamma and exponential use a **rate** (events per unit, larger means
shorter times); the Weibull table uses a **scale** (a typical time, larger means longer times); Chapter
25 rewrites the Weibull through its **hazard** with shape $\nu=k$ and coefficient
$\lambda(\mathbf{x})=\lambda^{-\nu}$. All three describe the same families with different symbols. A
Bayesian **precision** means the reciprocal of a variance, $1/\sigma^{2}$; the normal conjugacy of
@sec-dist-conjugacy adds precisions rather than variances.
{#tbl-dist-param}

## Discrete distributions {#sec-dist-discrete}

The four discrete families are defined in @def-bernoulli, @def-binomial, @def-poisson-binomial, and
@def-poisson. Their moment generating functions are finite for every $t\in\mathbb{R}$.

| Distribution | Support | Mass function $P(X=k)$ | $\mathbb{E}[X]$ | $\mathrm{Var}(X)$ | MGF $M_X(t)$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{Ber}(p)$, $\;p\in[0,1]$ | $\{0,1\}$ | $p^{k}(1-p)^{1-k}$ | $p$ | $p(1-p)$ | $(1-p)+pe^{t}$ |
| $\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$ | $\{0,1,\dots,n\}$ | $\binom{n}{k}p^{k}(1-p)^{n-k}$ | $np$ | $np(1-p)$ | $\big((1-p)+pe^{t}\big)^{n}$ |
| $\mathrm{PoBin}(\mathbf{p})$, $\;\mathbf{p}\in[0,1]^{n}$ | $\{0,1,\dots,n\}$ | $\displaystyle\sum_{\lvert S\rvert=k}\ \prod_{i\in S}p_i\prod_{i\notin S}(1-p_i)$ | $\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_i$ | $\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_i(1-p_i)$ | $\displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^{n}\big((1-p_i)+p_ie^{t}\big)$ |
| $\mathrm{Poi}(\lambda)$, $\;\lambda>0$ | $\{0,1,2,\dots\}$ | $e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{k}/k!$ | $\lambda$ | $\lambda$ | $\exp\!\big(\lambda(e^{t}-1)\big)$ |

: Discrete distributions used in the book. In the Poisson binomial row $S$ ranges over the
subsets of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ of size $k$, and the trial probabilities $p_i$ may differ.
{#tbl-dist-discrete}

Each family models a distinct kind of health data.

**Bernoulli.** A single yes/no outcome with success probability $p$: one patient, responder ($X=1$) or
non-responder ($X=0$). It is the atom from which the binary-outcome likelihoods of the book are built.

**Binomial.** The number of successes in $n$ independent, identical yes/no trials, each with the same
probability $p$: the count of responders out of $n$ randomized patients. This is the workhorse
likelihood for aggregate binary endpoints in meta-analysis (Chapter 13) and network meta-analysis, where
each arm reports "$r$ responders out of $n$."

**Poisson binomial.** The number of successes in $n$ independent trials whose success probabilities
$p_1,\dots,p_n$ are allowed to **differ**. The mass function looks forbidding but says something simple:
to get exactly $k$ successes, sum over every way of choosing which $k$ of the $n$ trials succeed, and for
each such choice multiply the success probabilities of the chosen trials by the failure probabilities of
the rest. It is the natural law for an aggregate event count when a model assigns each patient a
different predicted risk, which is exactly the situation in covariate-adjusted binary outcomes; it drives
the discrete aggregation results of @sec-pobin in Chapter 21.

**Poisson.** The count of events when events arrive independently at a constant average, for example the
number of relapses in a fixed follow-up window. In practice the Poisson mean is a **rate times an
exposure**: if events occur at rate $\rho$ per person-year and a patient is followed for time $E$, then
the event count is $\mathrm{Poi}(\rho E)$, so $\lambda=\rho E$. This is how Poisson models describe
events per person-time rather than bare counts.

The families nest. A Bernoulli variable is $\mathrm{Bin}(1,p)$; a binomial is the Poisson binomial with
all $p_i$ equal to a common $p$, in which case every entry of the Poisson binomial row reduces to its
binomial counterpart. The Poisson is the law of rare events: if $X_n\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,\lambda/n)$ then
$X_n\xrightarrow{d}\mathrm{Poi}(\lambda)$ (@thm-poisson-limit), so a Poisson is the limit of a binomial
with many trials each individually rare; a quantitative total-variation
form of this approximation drives the discrete aggregation results of Part V. Sums of independent
Poisson variables are Poisson, with rates adding, by the product rule for moment generating functions
(@thm-mgf-sum).

::: {.remark}
For a fixed mean $\sum_i p_i$, the Poisson binomial variance $\sum_i p_i(1-p_i)=\sum_i p_i-\sum_i
p_i^2$ is largest when the $p_i$ are equal, by convexity of $p\mapsto p^2$. (Convexity means
$\sum_i p_i^2$ is *smallest* when the $p_i$ are all equal, hence the variance
$\sum_i p_i-\sum_i p_i^2$ is *largest* there; pulling the risks apart only lowers the aggregate
variance.) Heterogeneous individual risks therefore produce a less dispersed aggregate count than a
binomial with the same expected number of events, a fact used when an aggregate event count is modeled
under covariate-adjusted risks. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#exm-dist-pobin}
## Aggregating three unequal risks
Suppose three patients have predicted event probabilities $p_1=0.1$, $p_2=0.3$, $p_3=0.6$, and we want
the distribution of the total number of events $X\sim\mathrm{PoBin}(0.1,0.3,0.6)$. Reading the Poisson
binomial mass function one value of $k$ at a time,
$$
\begin{aligned}
P(X=0)&=(0.9)(0.7)(0.4)=0.252,\\
P(X=1)&=(0.1)(0.7)(0.4)+(0.9)(0.3)(0.4)+(0.9)(0.7)(0.6)=0.514,\\
P(X=2)&=(0.1)(0.3)(0.4)+(0.1)(0.7)(0.6)+(0.9)(0.3)(0.6)=0.216,\\
P(X=3)&=(0.1)(0.3)(0.6)=0.018,
\end{aligned}
$$
which sum to $1$. The mean is $\mathbb{E}[X]=0.1+0.3+0.6=1.0$ and the variance is
$\mathrm{Var}(X)=0.1(0.9)+0.3(0.7)+0.6(0.4)=0.54$. Compare a binomial with the same mean, namely
$\mathrm{Bin}(3,\tfrac13)$, whose variance is $3\cdot\tfrac13\cdot\tfrac23=\tfrac23\approx0.667$. The
heterogeneous risks give the smaller variance $0.54<0.667$, exactly the effect of the remark above: when
predicted risks differ across patients the aggregate event count is less dispersed than a binomial with
the same expected number of events. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

When there are more than two response categories, the binomial generalizes to the **multinomial**, which
the appendix uses only as the likelihood conjugate to the Dirichlet of @sec-dist-dirichlet.

::: {#def-dist-multinomial}
## Multinomial distribution
Fix $N\in\{1,2,\dots\}$ and a probability vector $\mathbf{p}=(p_1,\dots,p_K)$ with $p_k\ge 0$ and
$\sum_{k=1}^{K}p_k=1$. The count vector $\mathbf{n}=(n_1,\dots,n_K)$ of the outcomes of $N$ independent
trials, each landing in category $k$ with probability $p_k$, has the **multinomial distribution**
$\mathrm{Multinomial}(N,\mathbf{p})$, with mass function
$$
P(\mathbf{n})=\binom{N}{n_1,\dots,n_K}\prod_{k=1}^{K}p_k^{\,n_k}
=\frac{N!}{n_1!\cdots n_K!}\prod_{k=1}^{K}p_k^{\,n_k},
\qquad \sum_{k=1}^{K}n_k=N,
$$ {#eq-dist-multinomial}
on the set of nonnegative integer vectors summing to $N$.
:::

The multinomial is the count of how many of $N$ patients fall into each of $K$ response categories, for
example none, partial, or complete response. It records the joint distribution of category counts, so a
single component $n_k$ is $\mathrm{Bin}(N,p_k)$ and at $K=2$ the whole family reduces to
$\mathrm{Bin}(N,p_1)$. Its first two moments are
$$
\mathbb{E}[n_k]=N p_k,\qquad \mathrm{Var}(n_k)=N p_k(1-p_k),\qquad
\mathrm{Cov}(n_j,n_k)=-N p_j p_k\ (j\neq k),
$$
the negative covariance reflecting that the counts must sum to $N$, so a surplus in one category forces a
deficit in another. This is the likelihood in the Dirichlet-multinomial conjugate pair of
@tbl-dist-conjugacy.

## Continuous univariate distributions {#sec-dist-continuous}

The normal density and its moments are @def-normal. The remaining four families are first used here; the
gamma and exponential appear as the conjugate prior and count-data baseline of Chapter 8 and as survival
baselines in Chapters 25 and 26, the Weibull is the power-law-hazard survival model of @sec-genlik-survival in
Chapter 25, and the beta is the conjugate prior of @thm-conjugate-beta-binomial. The gamma function
$\Gamma$ and beta function $B$ are those of @eq-dist-gamma-function and @eq-dist-beta-function.

| Distribution | Support | Density $f(x)$ | $\mathbb{E}[X]$ | $\mathrm{Var}(X)$ | MGF $M_X(t)$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2})$, $\;\sigma^{2}>0$ | $\mathbb{R}$ | $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma}\exp\!\Big(-\dfrac{(x-\mu)^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\Big)$ | $\mu$ | $\sigma^{2}$ | $\exp\!\big(\mu t+\tfrac12\sigma^{2}t^{2}\big)$ |
| $\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$, $\;\lambda>0$ (rate) | $(0,\infty)$ | $\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$ | $1/\lambda$ | $1/\lambda^{2}$ | $\dfrac{\lambda}{\lambda-t}$, $\;t<\lambda$ |
| $\mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha,\beta)$, shape $\alpha>0$, rate $\beta>0$ | $(0,\infty)$ | $\dfrac{\beta^{\alpha}}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\,x^{\alpha-1}e^{-\beta x}$ | $\alpha/\beta$ | $\alpha/\beta^{2}$ | $\Big(1-\dfrac{t}{\beta}\Big)^{-\alpha}$, $\;t<\beta$ |
| $\mathrm{Beta}(a,b)$, $\;a,b>0$ | $(0,1)$ | $\dfrac{1}{B(a,b)}\,x^{a-1}(1-x)^{b-1}$ | $\dfrac{a}{a+b}$ | $\dfrac{ab}{(a+b)^{2}(a+b+1)}$ | ${}_1F_1(a;a+b;t)$, no elementary form |
| $\mathrm{Weib}(k,\lambda)$, shape $k>0$, scale $\lambda>0$ | $(0,\infty)$ | $\dfrac{k}{\lambda}\Big(\dfrac{x}{\lambda}\Big)^{k-1}\!\exp\!\big(-(x/\lambda)^{k}\big)$ | $\lambda\,\Gamma\!\big(1+\tfrac1k\big)$ | $\lambda^{2}\big[\Gamma\!\big(1+\tfrac2k\big)-\Gamma\!\big(1+\tfrac1k\big)^{2}\big]$ | no elementary form |

: Continuous univariate distributions used in the book. The exponential and gamma moment generating
functions are finite only for $t$ below the rate; the others are discussed in the text.
{#tbl-dist-continuous}

Several entries deserve comment. In modeling terms the four non-normal families split cleanly by role:
the exponential and Weibull model **time-to-event** outcomes (overall or progression-free survival),
the gamma is a **prior on a positive rate or precision**, and the beta is a **prior on a probability**;
the normal models a **continuous endpoint** and, on the log scale, an estimated relative effect.

**Exponential and gamma.** The exponential is the gamma of unit shape, $\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)=
\mathrm{Gamma}(1,\lambda)$, as the densities and moment generating functions show. It is the simplest
time-to-event model, the one with a **constant hazard**: the instantaneous event rate does not change
over time, so the exponential is **memoryless**, meaning a patient who has survived to time $s$ has the
same remaining-life distribution as a fresh patient ($P(X>s+u\mid X>s)=P(X>u)$). Because independent
moment generating functions multiply (@thm-mgf-sum), a sum of $n$ independent $\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$
variables has MGF $(1-t/\lambda)^{-n}$, hence is $\mathrm{Gamma}(n,\lambda)$; more generally gammas with
a common rate add in shape. The chi-square law with $\nu$ degrees of freedom is
$\mathrm{Gamma}(\nu/2,\,1/2)$. The gamma is the book's default prior on a positive quantity such as a
Poisson rate (@prp-conjugate-gamma-poisson) or a precision; its shape parameter $\alpha$ sets the shape
of the density, with $\alpha<1$ giving a density that diverges at the origin and decreases, $\alpha=1$
the exponential, and $\alpha>1$ a unimodal density that starts at zero, rises to a peak, and decays. The
MGF $(1-t/\beta)^{-\alpha}$ is finite precisely for $t<\beta$ and
diverges as $t\uparrow\beta$, the right tail being too heavy to integrate against $e^{tx}$ beyond that
point (for $t\ge\beta$ the defining integral $\int_0^\infty e^{tx}f(x)\,dx$ diverges because
$e^{tx}e^{-\beta x}$ no longer decays); all moments are nonetheless finite, with
$\mathbb{E}[X^{r}]=\Gamma(\alpha+r)/\big(\beta^{r}\Gamma(\alpha)\big)$ for $r>-\alpha$.

**Beta.** The single most useful fact for a health researcher is that the beta puts a flexible
distribution on a **probability**: because its support is $(0,1)$, it is the natural prior on a response
rate, and it is the conjugate prior for the binomial (@thm-conjugate-beta-binomial). Its two parameters
read as **pseudo-counts**: $a$ behaves like a number of prior successes and $b$ like a number of prior
failures, so the prior mean $a/(a+b)$ is the prior success fraction and larger $a+b$ means a more
concentrated, more confident prior. As a shape guide: $a=b=1$ is the uniform law on $(0,1)$ (no prior
information); $a=b>1$ is symmetric and unimodal at $\tfrac12$; $a>b$ leans toward $1$ and $a<b$ toward
$0$; and $a,b<1$ is U-shaped, piling mass near the two endpoints. The density is bounded with compact
support, so the MGF is finite for every $t$, but it has no elementary closed form. *(Advanced; you will
not use the beta MGF in practice, since the moments below are elementary and are what the book uses.)*
The MGF equals the confluent hypergeometric function
$$
M_X(t)={}_1F_1(a;a+b;t)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(a)_n}{(a+b)_n}\frac{t^{n}}{n!},\qquad
(c)_n:=c(c+1)\cdots(c+n-1),
$$ {#eq-dist-beta-mgf}
where $(c)_n$ is the rising factorial (Pochhammer symbol). Moments are elementary even though the MGF is
not: $\mathbb{E}[X^{r}]=B(a+r,b)/B(a,b)=\Gamma(a+r)\Gamma(a+b)\big/\big(\Gamma(a)\Gamma(a+b+r)\big)$ for
$r>-a$, which gives the mean and variance in @tbl-dist-continuous. The case $a=b=1$ is the uniform law
on $(0,1)$.

**Weibull.** The survival function is $S(x)=\exp(-(x/\lambda)^{k})$ and the hazard is
$h(x)=\frac{k}{\lambda}(x/\lambda)^{k-1}$, a power law in $x$. The shape parameter $k$ controls whether
risk rises or falls over time, which is exactly what a clinician chooses a survival model to capture:
$k<1$ gives a **decreasing** hazard (early high risk that wanes, the "infant mortality" pattern), $k=1$
gives a **constant** hazard (the exponential), and $k>1$ gives an **increasing** hazard (risk that
grows with time, the "aging" or wear-out pattern). The $r$-th moment is
$\mathbb{E}[X^{r}]=\lambda^{r}\Gamma(1+r/k)$, from which the tabulated mean and variance follow. With
$k=1$ the hazard is constant and the Weibull is the exponential with rate $1/\lambda$. The moment
generating function has no elementary closed form and, more sharply, is finite on a neighborhood of the
origin only when $k\ge 1$: for $k<1$ the tail $\exp(-(x/\lambda)^{k})$ decays slower than any
exponential, so $\mathbb{E}[e^{tX}]=\infty$ for every $t>0$ and the MGF does not exist, though all
polynomial moments remain finite. (The reason $k<1$ makes the tail slow is that the exponent
$(x/\lambda)^{k}$ then grows *sub-linearly* in $x$, so $e^{-(x/\lambda)^{k}}$ falls off more slowly than
$e^{-cx}$ for any $c>0$.)

::: {#exm-dist-weibull}
## How the Weibull shape bends the hazard
Fix the scale $\lambda=1$ and read the hazard $h(x)=k\,x^{k-1}$ at three follow-up times for three
shapes. The table gives $h(x)$ at $x=0.25,\ 1,\ 4$.

| Shape $k$ | $h(0.25)$ | $h(1)$ | $h(4)$ | Hazard over time |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $0.5$ | $1.00$ | $0.50$ | $0.25$ | decreasing (early risk wanes) |
| $1$ | $1.00$ | $1.00$ | $1.00$ | constant (exponential, memoryless) |
| $2$ | $0.50$ | $2.00$ | $8.00$ | increasing (risk grows with time) |

With $k=0.5$ the event rate is highest just after baseline and falls; with $k=1$ it never changes; with
$k=2$ it climbs steadily. The three hazards differ at $x=\lambda=1$ ($h(1)=k$), but their cumulative
hazards agree there, $H(\lambda)=(\lambda/\lambda)^{k}=1$, so $S(\lambda)=e^{-1}\approx0.37$ for every
shape: the scale is the time by which about $63\%$ of patients have had the event, and the shape sets the
tilt of the hazard. This is the
single most important reading of a Weibull survival model: the shape $k$ is chosen to match whether a
clinical hazard rises or falls with time. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Hazard parametrization.** Chapter 25 writes the Weibull through its hazard,
$h(t\mid\mathbf{x})=\lambda(\mathbf{x})\,\nu\,t^{\nu-1}$, giving the survival function
$S(t\mid\mathbf{x})=\exp(-\lambda(\mathbf{x})\,t^{\nu})$ (see @sec-genlik-survival). This is the shape-scale form
above with shape $k=\nu$ and scale $\lambda=\lambda(\mathbf{x})^{-1/\nu}$, equivalently
$\lambda(\mathbf{x})=\lambda^{-\nu}$. The two parametrizations describe the same family; the
hazard form places the covariate structure on the rate-type coefficient $\lambda(\mathbf{x})$, which is
convenient for proportional-hazards regression. See @tbl-dist-param for the three survival
parametrizations side by side. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## The multivariate normal {#sec-dist-mvn}

The multivariate normal $\mathcal{N}_p(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})$ is defined in @def-mvn
through its moment generating function and is developed in full in @sec-mvn of Chapter 4. We restate the
core formulas and point to the chapter for proofs. In this book the family plays four roles: it models a
vector of correlated **baseline covariates** in a trial population (Chapters 12 and 20); it is the prior
for a vector of **random effects** in a hierarchical model (Chapter 8); it is the approximate
**sampling distribution** of a vector of estimated log-effects fed into network meta-analysis (Chapters
13 and 15); and, through the Gaussian copula, it is the engine that ties marginal covariate
distributions together for the **ML-NMR numerical integration** of Chapter 22 (@sec-qmc-gaussian).
Throughout, $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\succ 0$ means $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ is positive definite, which is the
condition under which the covariance is invertible and a density exists.

| Quantity | Formula | Reference |
|---|---|---|
| Support | $\mathbb{R}^{p}$; density exists on $\mathbb{R}^{p}$ when $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\succ 0$ | @def-mvn |
| Density ($\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\succ 0$) | $(2\pi)^{-p/2}\det(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})^{-1/2}\exp\!\big(-\tfrac12(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\big)$ | @prp-mvn-density, @eq-mvn-density |
| Mean | $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ | @def-mvn |
| Covariance | $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ | @def-mvn |
| MGF | $\exp\!\big(\mathbf{t}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\mu}+\tfrac12\,\mathbf{t}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\,\mathbf{t}\big)$, all $\mathbf{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ | @eq-mvn-mgf |

: The multivariate normal $\mathcal{N}_p(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})$ with mean
$\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and positive semidefinite covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$.
{#tbl-dist-mvn}

The family is closed under the operations that drive normal-theory inference, proved in Chapter 4.

- **Affine maps.** If $\mathbf{X}\sim\mathcal{N}_p(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})$ and
  $\mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{b}+B\mathbf{X}$, then
  $\mathbf{Y}\sim\mathcal{N}_q(\mathbf{b}+B\boldsymbol{\mu},\,B\boldsymbol{\Sigma}B^{\top})$
  (@thm-mvn-linear). In particular every subvector is multivariate normal and every linear combination
  $\mathbf{a}^{\top}\mathbf{X}$ is univariate normal.
- **Uncorrelated implies independent.** Jointly normal blocks with zero cross-covariance are
  independent (@lem-normal-uncorrelated-independent), a property special to the normal family.
- **Conditioning.** With $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}\succ 0$,
  $$
  \mathbf{X}_1\mid\mathbf{X}_2=\mathbf{x}_2\ \sim\
  \mathcal{N}\!\Big(\boldsymbol{\mu}_1+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}
  (\mathbf{x}_2-\boldsymbol{\mu}_2),\ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11}-\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}
  \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{21}\Big),
  $$
  the conditional mean affine in $\mathbf{x}_2$ and the conditional covariance, the Schur complement of
  $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}$, free of $\mathbf{x}_2$ (@thm-mvn-conditional, @eq-mvn-conditional).

The conditioning formula is best read as a **linear regression of $\mathbf{X}_1$ on $\mathbf{X}_2$**: the
conditional mean is the prediction $\boldsymbol{\mu}_1+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}
(\mathbf{x}_2-\boldsymbol{\mu}_2)$ with regression-coefficient matrix
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}$, and the conditional covariance (the term some
readers know as the Schur complement, which you may take as a name on a first pass) does not depend on
the observed value $\mathbf{x}_2$, so observing $\mathbf{X}_2$ shifts the center of $\mathbf{X}_1$ but
does not change its spread. This is precisely what one needs to impute an unreported baseline covariate
from reported ones in a population-adjustment problem.

::: {#exm-dist-mvn-predict}
## Predicting a missing covariate from an observed one
Let $(X_1,X_2)$ be bivariate normal with means $\mu_1=\mu_2=0$, unit variances, and correlation
$\rho=0.6$, so $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}=\rho=0.6$ and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}=1$. Suppose $X_1$ (say a
baseline covariate not reported by a study) is unknown but the correlated covariate $X_2=2$ is observed.
The conditioning formula gives
$$
X_1\mid X_2=2\ \sim\ \mathcal{N}\big(\rho\cdot 2,\ 1-\rho^{2}\big)=\mathcal{N}(1.2,\ 0.64).
$$
The predicted mean $1.2$ is the regression of $X_1$ on $X_2$ with slope $\rho=0.6$, and the conditional
variance $0.64$ is smaller than the marginal variance $1$: knowing the correlated covariate sharpens the
prediction. The conditional variance $1-\rho^{2}$ would be the same whatever value of $X_2$ we had
observed. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The univariate normal is the case $p=1$, and the standard normal $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$, with density $\phi$
and distribution function $\Phi$, is treated in @sec-dist-standard-normal.

## The Dirichlet distribution {#sec-dist-dirichlet}

The Dirichlet is the distribution of a random probability vector and is the multivariate generalization
of the beta. In one line: it is a **prior for a list of probabilities that must add up to one**, such as
the probabilities of the response categories none, partial, and complete. It is the natural conjugate
prior for the cell probabilities of a categorical or multinomial outcome (@def-dist-multinomial),
generalizing the beta-binomial pair of @thm-conjugate-beta-binomial.

::: {#def-dist-dirichlet}
## Dirichlet distribution
Let $\boldsymbol{\alpha}=(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_K)$ with each $\alpha_k>0$, and write
$\alpha_0=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\alpha_k$. A random vector
$\mathbf{X}=(X_1,\dots,X_K)$ supported on the open simplex
$\Delta^{K-1}=\{\mathbf{x}:x_k>0,\ \sum_{k=1}^{K}x_k=1\}$ has the **Dirichlet distribution**
$\mathrm{Dir}(\boldsymbol{\alpha})$ if it has density
$$
f(\mathbf{x})=\frac{1}{B(\boldsymbol{\alpha})}\prod_{k=1}^{K}x_k^{\alpha_k-1},
\qquad B(\boldsymbol{\alpha})=\frac{\prod_{k=1}^{K}\Gamma(\alpha_k)}{\Gamma(\alpha_0)},
$$ {#eq-dist-dirichlet-density}
with respect to Lebesgue measure on the $(K-1)$-dimensional simplex, taking $x_1,\dots,x_{K-1}$ as free
coordinates and $x_K=1-\sum_{k<K}x_k$.
:::

The **simplex** $\Delta^{K-1}$ is just the set of valid probability vectors: $K$ nonnegative numbers that
add to one. *(Advanced; skip on a first pass.)* The phrase "density with respect to Lebesgue measure on
the $(K-1)$-dimensional simplex, taking $x_1,\dots,x_{K-1}$ as free coordinates" means only that we treat
$x_1,\dots,x_{K-1}$ as the free variables, with the last coordinate forced to be
$x_K=1-\sum_{k<K}x_k$, and integrate over those $K-1$ free variables. The normalizing constant
$B(\boldsymbol{\alpha})$ is the multivariate beta function of @eq-dist-beta-function, the product-of-gammas
generalization of the scalar $B(a,b)$.

The simplex constraint $\sum_k X_k=1$ forces the components to be negatively associated and makes the
joint moment generating function on $\mathbb{R}^{K}$ degenerate, so the Dirichlet is described by its
moments rather than by an MGF (this is the hyperplane degeneracy explained in @sec-dist-conventions). The
mixed moments are
$$
\mathbb{E}\!\Big[\prod_{k=1}^{K}X_k^{r_k}\Big]
=\frac{B(\boldsymbol{\alpha}+\mathbf{r})}{B(\boldsymbol{\alpha})}
=\frac{\Gamma(\alpha_0)}{\Gamma(\alpha_0+\textstyle\sum_k r_k)}\prod_{k=1}^{K}
\frac{\Gamma(\alpha_k+r_k)}{\Gamma(\alpha_k)},
$$ {#eq-dist-dirichlet-moments}
from which the first two moments follow.

| Quantity | Formula |
|---|---|
| Support | $\Delta^{K-1}=\{\mathbf{x}:x_k>0,\ \sum_k x_k=1\}$ |
| Density | $\dfrac{1}{B(\boldsymbol{\alpha})}\prod_{k=1}^{K}x_k^{\alpha_k-1}$ |
| Mean | $\mathbb{E}[X_k]=\alpha_k/\alpha_0$ |
| Variance | $\mathrm{Var}(X_k)=\dfrac{\alpha_k(\alpha_0-\alpha_k)}{\alpha_0^{2}(\alpha_0+1)}$ |
| Covariance | $\mathrm{Cov}(X_j,X_k)=\dfrac{-\alpha_j\alpha_k}{\alpha_0^{2}(\alpha_0+1)}$, $\;j\neq k$ |
| MGF | degenerate (support in the hyperplane $\sum_k x_k=1$); use @eq-dist-dirichlet-moments |

: The Dirichlet distribution $\mathrm{Dir}(\boldsymbol{\alpha})$ on the simplex $\Delta^{K-1}$, with
$\alpha_0=\sum_k\alpha_k$.
{#tbl-dist-dirichlet}

With $K=2$ and $\boldsymbol{\alpha}=(a,b)$ the first coordinate $X_1$ is $\mathrm{Beta}(a,b)$, so the
beta entries of @tbl-dist-continuous are the $K=2$ case of @tbl-dist-dirichlet. The parameters read as
**pseudo-counts**, exactly as for the beta: $\alpha_k$ is a prior count for category $k$, and the total
$\alpha_0=\sum_k\alpha_k$ is a **concentration**. The mean is $\alpha_k/\alpha_0$ regardless of
$\alpha_0$, while the variances and covariances shrink as $\alpha_0$ grows. The picture: a small
$\alpha_0$ spreads the random probability vector out toward the corners of the simplex (nearly all mass
on one category, but which one varies), while a large $\alpha_0$ clusters it tightly around the mean
vector $(\alpha_1/\alpha_0,\dots,\alpha_K/\alpha_0)$. Concentration is thus the multivariate reading of
"how confident is the prior," the same role $a+b$ plays for the beta.

## The standard normal function and density {#sec-dist-standard-normal}

The standard normal $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ is the case $\mu=0,\ \sigma^{2}=1$ of @def-normal. Its density and
distribution function carry the dedicated symbols $\phi$ and $\Phi$:
$$
\phi(z)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\,e^{-z^{2}/2},\qquad
\Phi(z)=\int_{-\infty}^{z}\phi(u)\,du,\qquad z\in\mathbb{R}.
$$ {#eq-dist-phi}
The density $\phi$ is even and satisfies the differential identities
$$
\phi'(z)=-z\,\phi(z),\qquad \phi''(z)=(z^{2}-1)\,\phi(z),\qquad \Phi'(z)=\phi(z),
$$ {#eq-dist-phi-derivs}
and the distribution function satisfies $\Phi(0)=\tfrac12$, the reflection identity
$\Phi(-z)=1-\Phi(z)$, and the limits $\Phi(z)\to 1$ as $z\to\infty$ and $\Phi(z)\to 0$ as
$z\to-\infty$. The mean and variance are $\mathbb{E}[Z]=0$ and $\mathrm{Var}(Z)=1$, the moment
generating function is $M_Z(t)=e^{t^{2}/2}$, finite for all $t$, and the moments are
$$
\mathbb{E}[Z^{2m-1}]=0,\qquad \mathbb{E}[Z^{2m}]=\frac{(2m)!}{2^{m}m!}=(2m-1)!!,\qquad m=1,2,\dots,
$$ {#eq-dist-normal-moments}
read off as the Taylor coefficients of $e^{t^{2}/2}=\sum_{m\ge 0}t^{2m}/(2^{m}m!)$ through
@thm-mgf-moments.

There is no elementary closed form for $\Phi$. It is expressed through the **error function**
$\mathrm{erf}(x)=\frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}}\int_0^{x}e^{-u^{2}}\,du$ and its complement
$\mathrm{erfc}=1-\mathrm{erf}$ by
$$
\Phi(z)=\tfrac12\Big[1+\mathrm{erf}\!\big(z/\sqrt{2}\big)\Big],\qquad
1-\Phi(z)=\tfrac12\,\mathrm{erfc}\!\big(z/\sqrt{2}\big),
$$ {#eq-dist-Phi-erf}
whose numerical evaluation is treated in [Appendix D](/appendices/D-special-functions.qmd). *(Advanced;
optional on a first pass.)* For the upper tail the Mills ratio gives the two-sided bound, valid for
$z>0$,
$$
\Big(\frac{1}{z}-\frac{1}{z^{3}}\Big)\phi(z)\ <\ 1-\Phi(z)\ <\ \frac{\phi(z)}{z},
$$ {#eq-dist-mills}
so that $1-\Phi(z)\sim \phi(z)/z$ as $z\to\infty$. This bound matters because $1-\Phi(z)$ is the tail
probability of a standardized effect, so it controls how fast $p$-values and normal-approximation tail
probabilities for large standardized effects decay; a novice can note the asymptotic
$1-\Phi(z)\sim\phi(z)/z$ and move on.

The function $\Phi$ also feeds two constructions the book uses later. It is the inverse link of the
**probit regression model** (Chapter 7), the model in which a binary probability is written
$P(Y=1)=\Phi(\eta)$ for a linear predictor $\eta$. And its inverse $\Phi^{-1}$ is the **normal quantile
transform** at the heart of the Gaussian copula
$C_\Omega(\mathbf{u})=\Phi_\Omega\big(\Phi^{-1}(u_1),\dots,\Phi^{-1}(u_d)\big)$ used in ML-NMR numerical
integration: given a uniform variable $u\in(0,1)$, the value $\Phi^{-1}(u)$ is the standard-normal score
with that lower-tail probability, so $\Phi^{-1}$ turns the uniform points of a quasi-Monte Carlo rule
into correlated normal covariate draws over which an individual likelihood is averaged (@sec-qmc-pit,
@sec-qmc-gaussian). See [Notation](/notation.qmd) for the copula symbol.

## Conjugate pairs {#sec-dist-conjugacy}

A prior family is *conjugate* to a likelihood when the posterior stays in the family with updated
hyperparameters. Conjugacy is an **algebraic convenience**, not a requirement of Bayesian modeling: it
makes the update a closed-form parameter change instead of a numerical integration, but a valid Bayesian
analysis may use any proper prior (and the book's hierarchical models in Chapter 8 and Chapter 24 mostly
use non-conjugate priors sampled by Markov chain Monte Carlo). Chapter 8 proves the three pairs of
@sec-conjugacy in full and uses them to build the
shrinkage estimator and the Gibbs updates of its samplers. @tbl-dist-conjugacy collects those pairs,
together with the Dirichlet-multinomial pair that generalizes the beta-binomial; throughout, the gamma
prior uses the shape-rate parametrization, so $\mathrm{Gamma}(a,b)$ has mean $a/b$.

| Prior | Likelihood (data model) | Posterior | Reference |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\theta\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_0,\tau_0^{2})$ | $y\mid\theta\sim\mathcal{N}(\theta,\sigma^{2})$, $\sigma^{2}$ known | $\theta\mid y\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_1,\tau_1^{2})$, $\tau_1^{-2}=\tau_0^{-2}+\sigma^{-2}$ | @thm-conjugate-normal |
| $\boldsymbol{\theta}\sim\mathcal{N}_p(\mathbf{m}_0,\boldsymbol{\Omega}_0)$ | $\mathbf{y}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta}\sim\mathcal{N}_p(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})$, $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ known | $\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\mathbf{y}\sim\mathcal{N}_p(\mathbf{m}_1,\boldsymbol{\Omega}_1)$, $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_1^{-1}=\boldsymbol{\Omega}_0^{-1}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}$ | @cor-conjugate-normal-mv |
| $p\sim\mathrm{Beta}(a,b)$ | $y\mid p\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$ | $p\mid y\sim\mathrm{Beta}(a+y,\,b+n-y)$ | @thm-conjugate-beta-binomial |
| $\lambda\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(a,b)$ | $y_i\mid\lambda\sim\mathrm{Poi}(\lambda)$ iid | $\lambda\mid\mathbf{y}\sim\mathrm{Gamma}\!\big(a+\sum_i y_i,\ b+n\big)$ | @prp-conjugate-gamma-poisson |
| $\mathbf{p}\sim\mathrm{Dir}(\boldsymbol{\alpha})$ | $\mathbf{n}\mid\mathbf{p}\sim\mathrm{Multinomial}(N,\mathbf{p})$ | $\mathbf{p}\mid\mathbf{n}\sim\mathrm{Dir}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}+\mathbf{n})$ | generalizes @thm-conjugate-beta-binomial |

: Conjugate prior-likelihood pairs. The first four are proved in @sec-conjugacy of Chapter 8; the
Dirichlet-multinomial pair is the standard $K$-category generalization of the beta-binomial pair, with
the beta-binomial recovered at $K=2$.
{#tbl-dist-conjugacy}

In each row the posterior hyperparameters combine prior information with data additively. For the
normal-normal pair **precisions** (the reciprocals of the variances) add, and the posterior mean is the
precision-weighted average of prior mean and data (@eq-conjugate-normal): if the prior says the effect is
about $\mu_0$ and the data say about $y$, the posterior mean sits between them, pulled toward whichever is
more precise. For the beta-binomial and Dirichlet-multinomial pairs the prior
hyperparameters act as pseudo-counts that are incremented by the observed counts (@eq-conjugate-beta);
and for the gamma-Poisson pair the shape is incremented by the total count and the rate by the number of
observations. The posterior mean is in every case a convex combination of the prior mean and the
maximum likelihood estimate, the analytic form of shrinkage that Chapter 8 develops.

::: {#exm-dist-betabinom}
## A beta-binomial update with numbers
Put a uniform prior $\mathrm{Beta}(1,1)$ on a response probability $p$ (the flat prior: every value in
$(0,1)$ equally likely, prior mean $\tfrac12$). Observe $y=7$ responders out of $n=10$ patients. By the
beta-binomial row of @tbl-dist-conjugacy the posterior is
$$
p\mid y\ \sim\ \mathrm{Beta}(1+7,\ 1+10-7)=\mathrm{Beta}(8,4),
$$
with posterior mean $8/(8+4)=8/12=2/3\approx0.667$. The two prior pseudo-counts $a=b=1$ have been
incremented by the $7$ observed successes and $3$ observed failures. Contrast the maximum likelihood
estimate $\hat p=7/10=0.7$ and the prior mean $0.5$: the posterior mean $0.667$ lies between them, and
is in fact their convex combination
$$
\frac{a+b}{a+b+n}\cdot\frac12+\frac{n}{a+b+n}\cdot\frac{y}{n}
=\frac{2}{12}\cdot 0.5+\frac{10}{12}\cdot 0.7=0.667,
$$
weighted toward the data because the flat prior carries only $a+b=2$ pseudo-observations against $n=10$
real ones. This is the shrinkage reading of the closing paragraph, made concrete. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why the inverse-gamma is not cataloged.** The classical conjugate prior for the variance $\sigma^{2}$
of a normal likelihood with known mean is the **inverse-gamma** (a gamma law on the precision
$1/\sigma^{2}$). This book does not use it: for the between-study variance of a hierarchical model the
text follows modern practice and places a half-normal or half-$t$ prior on the between-study standard
deviation (Chapter 8; @dias2018nma), which behaves better when the variance may be near zero, where an
inverse-gamma prior is unstable. The inverse-gamma is therefore mentioned here only so a reader does not
search the tables for it. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Notes and references {#sec-dist-notes}

The catalogue draws on the following sources; each family points back to where it is derived or used.

- **Bernoulli, binomial, Poisson binomial, Poisson, normal, and multivariate normal**: mass functions,
  densities, means, variances, and moment generating functions, with derivations, are in
  @sec-distributions and @sec-mvn of Chapter 4.
- **Moment generating function properties** that justify the MGF columns are @thm-mgf-moments (moments by
  differentiation) and @thm-mgf-uniqueness (the MGF determines the law), the latter relying on the
  inversion of the characteristic function (@billingsley1995, §29 to §30).
- **Gamma, beta, exponential, Weibull, Dirichlet, multinomial** and the gamma and beta special functions
  are standard; a measure-theoretic treatment is @billingsley1995, and the special-function evaluations
  are collected in [Appendix D](/appendices/D-special-functions.qmd).
- **Conjugate pairs and their shrinkage reading** are proved in @sec-conjugacy of Chapter 8; the
  half-normal and half-$t$ priors preferred over the inverse-gamma for heterogeneity variances are
  discussed in Chapter 8 and @dias2018nma.
- **Hazard parametrization** of the Weibull and exponential, used for survival baselines, is that of
  @sec-genlik-survival in Chapter 25 and of @phillippo2025general.
- **Standard normal in numerical integration**: the probability integral transform and the Gaussian
  copula that consume $\Phi$ and $\Phi^{-1}$ are @sec-qmc-pit and @sec-qmc-gaussian of Chapter 22.
